claim: Dendritic cells (DCs) regulate processes ranging from antitumor and antiviral immunity to host-microbe communication at mucosal surfaces.
source: Dendritic cells (DCs) regulate processes ranging from antitumor and antiviral immunity to host-microbe communication at mucosal surfaces.
evidence: This is a general statement about DC function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: It remains difficult to genetically manipulate human DCs.
source: It remains difficult, however, to genetically manipulate human DCs, limiting our ability to probe how DCs elicit specific immune responses.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of the field and is supported by the context of the manuscript describing the need for new methods.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing method for human monocyte-derived DCs mediates knockouts with a median efficiency of >94% across >300 genes.
source: Here, we develop a CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing method for human monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) that mediates knockouts with a median efficiency of >94% across >300 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the genetic screen presented in the manuscript.

claim: The method enables genetic screens in moDCs to identify mechanisms by which DCs tune responses to lipopolysaccharides from the human microbiome.
source: Using this method, we perform genetic screens in moDCs, identifying mechanisms by which DCs tune responses to lipopolysaccharides from the human microbiome.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: The study reveals donor-specific responses to lipopolysaccharides.
source: In addition, we reveal donor-specific responses to lipopolysaccharides, underscoring the importance of assessing immune phenotypes in donor-derived cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations across multiple donors showing variation in LPS responses.

claim: The study identifies candidate genes that control donor-specific responses to lipopolysaccharides.
source: and identify candidate genes that control this specificity, highlighting the potential of our method to pinpoint determinants of inter-individual variation in immunity.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic screen data identifying genes like PTPN6 that show donor-specific effects.

claim: DCs act as sentinels, detecting invaders and initiating innate immune responses to clear them.
source: they act as sentinels, detecting invaders and initiating innate immune responses to clear them
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC function cited in the context of the introduction.

claim: DCs act as antigen-presenting cells, initiating adaptive immune responses that are antigen-specific and tailored to the context in which the antigen was detected.
source: and as antigen-presenting cells, initiating adaptive immune responses that are antigen-specific and tailored to the context in which the antigen was detected (Merad et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC function supported by citations to the literature.

claim: DCs mediate pathogen clearance, tumor cell killing, and tolerance to microbiome bacteria or dietary antigens.
source: In this fashion, DCs mediate pathogen clearance, tumor cell killing, and tolerance to microbiome bacteria or dietary antigens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC function in the immune system.

claim: DCs play fundamental roles in shaping host-pathogen and host-microbiome interactions and in the etiology of autoimmune disorders.
source: DCs thus play fundamental roles in shaping host-pathogen and host-microbiome interactions and in the etiology of autoimmune disorders
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC function in immunity and disease.

claim: DCs are a major target for efforts to develop new generations of immunotherapies.
source: and are a major target for efforts to develop new generations of immunotherapies (Wculek et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature on DC-based immunotherapy.

claim: Dissecting the pathways by which human DCs respond to innate immune stimuli and relay them into adaptive responses has been challenging due to difficulties in genetically manipulating human DCs.
source: Dissecting the pathways by which human DCs respond to innate immune stimuli and relay them into adaptive responses, however, has been challenging, due in large part to difficulties in genetically manipulating human DCs.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field and provides context for the need for the developed method.

claim: Approaches for gene repression in human DCs by RNAi have been reported.
source: Although approaches for gene repression in human DCs by RNAi have been reported (Song, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on RNAi in DCs.

claim: RNAi suffers from limited efficacy and specificity, precluding broader implementation.
source: RNAi suffers from limited efficacy and specificity, precluding broader implementation (Kaelin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on limitations of RNAi.

claim: DC biology is generally studied in mouse models.
source: As a consequence, DC biology is generally studied in mouse models
evidence: This reflects common practice in the field.

claim: Mice and humans differ in many aspects of both innate and adaptive immunity, including innate immune receptor repertoires, responses to immune ligands such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and developmental pathways of adaptive immune cells.
source: but mice and humans differ in many aspects of both innate and adaptive immunity, including innate immune receptor repertoires, responses to immune ligands such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and developmental pathways of adaptive immune cells (Pulendran and Davis, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on differences between mouse and human immunity.

claim: One way to address the challenge of genetically manipulating human DCs is to knock out genes in DC precursor populations such as monocytes or stem cells, followed by differentiation into DCs.
source: One way to address this challenge is to knock out genes in DC precursor populations such as monocytes or stem cells, followed by differentiation into DCs (Freund et al., 2020; Hiatt et al., 2020; Laustsen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work using this approach.

claim: Methods that knock out genes in DC precursor populations require independent differentiation of each knockout population and are susceptible to batch effects and poorly suited for genetic screens.
source: These methods, however, require independent differentiation of each knockout population and as a result are susceptible to batch effects and poorly suited for genetic screens.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical limitations of the precursor knockout approach.

claim: Methods that knock out genes in DC precursor populations do not permit probing the functions of genes required for DC differentiation and culture.
source: Moreover, they do not permit probing the functions of genes required for DC differentiation and culture.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of knocking out genes before differentiation.

claim: Both animal and stem cell models fail to capture inter-individual variation in immune phenotypes.
source: More broadly, both animal and stem cell models fail to capture inter-individual variation in immune phenotypes (Sanz et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on inter-individual variation.

claim: Inter-individual variation in immune phenotypes has been observed in innate immune responses, autoimmunity, and pathogen susceptibility.
source: which has been observed for example in innate immune responses, autoimmunity, and pathogen susceptibility (Brodin and Davis, 2017; Fairfax et al., 2014; Ye et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature documenting inter-individual variation.

claim: Inter-individual variation in immune phenotypes has gained further salience during the Covid-19 pandemic.
source: and has gained further salience during the Covid-19 pandemic (Lucas et al., 2020; Pereira et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on COVID-19 immune responses.

claim: Inter-individual variation in immune phenotypes results from a combination of genetic factors and lifelong environmental exposures (e.g., from the microbiome).
source: Such variation results from a combination of genetic factors and lifelong environmental exposures (e.g., from the microbiome)
evidence: This is established knowledge about sources of immune variation.

claim: It remains challenging to define the causal determinants of inter-individual variation in immunity in the absence of genetic tools for patient-derived immune cells such as DCs.
source: but it remains challenging to define the causal determinants in the absence of genetic tools for patient-derived immune cells such as DCs.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of current approaches for studying inter-individual variation.

claim: The authors developed a CRISPR-Cas9 strategy to construct targeted knockouts directly in human monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs).
source: To address these limitations, we developed a CRISPR-Cas9 strategy to construct targeted knockouts directly in human monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs)
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: Human monocyte-derived DCs are readily derived from donor blood and are widely used for research and clinical applications.
source: which are readily derived from donor blood and are widely used for research and clinical applications (Sallusto and Lanzavecchia, 1994; Garg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about moDCs supported by citations.

claim: The authors conducted a genetic screen for factors that recognize an innate immune ligand from the human microbiome, LPS from the gut commensal Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (B. theta).
source: Using this strategy, we conducted a genetic screen for factors that recognize an innate immune ligand from the human microbiome, LPS from the gut commensal Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (B. theta)
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the genetic screen.

claim: The genetic screen recapitulated known LPS signaling pathways.
source: recapitulating known LPS signaling pathways
evidence: This is supported by the screen data showing expected hits in TLR4 signaling pathways.

claim: The genetic screen revealed candidate genes that mediate species-specific LPS recognition.
source: and revealing candidate genes that mediate species-specific LPS recognition
evidence: This is supported by the screen data identifying genes with differential effects on B. theta LPS versus E. coli LPS responses.

claim: The genetic screen revealed candidate genes that give rise to inter-individual variation in the response to LPS.
source: and give rise to inter-individual variation in the response to LPS.
evidence: This is supported by the screen data showing donor-specific effects of genes like PTPN6.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing strategy is based on electroporation of in vitro-assembled Cas9-sgRNA complexes (Cas9 ribonucleoprotein particles, RNPs).
source: To enable introduction of specific knockouts in human moDCs, we developed a non-viral genome editing strategy based on electroporation of in vitro-assembled Cas9-sgRNA complexes (Cas9 ribonucleoprotein particles, RNPs)
evidence: This describes the technical approach used in the manuscript.

claim: The RNP-based approach has been validated in other immune cell types.
source: an approach that has been validated in other immune cell types (Freund et al., 2020; Hiatt et al., 2020; Riggan et al., 2020; Roth et al., 2018; Schumann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work using RNP-based editing in immune cells.

claim: The strategy entails isolating monocytes from human donor blood, differentiating them into moDCs in the presence of GM-CSF and IL-4, and electroporating these moDCs with Cas9 RNPs to induce double-strand breaks at the targeted locus.
source: Briefly, our strategy entails isolating monocytes from human donor blood, differentiating them into moDCs in the presence of GM-CSF and IL-4, and electroporating these moDCs with Cas9 RNPs to induce double-strand breaks at the targeted locus (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental workflow shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Double-strand breaks trigger error-prone DNA repair and subsequent formation of insertions or deletions (indels) that, with a certain frequency, cause frameshift mutations and thus knockout of the targeted gene.
source: Such double-strand breaks trigger error-prone DNA repair and subsequent formation of insertions or deletions (indels) that, with a certain frequency, cause frameshift mutations and thus knockout of the targeted gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism.

claim: The efficiency of genome editing is monitored by genotyping using next-generation sequencing and by phenotyping using functional assays.
source: We monitor the efficiency of this process by genotyping using next-generation sequencing and by phenotyping using functional assays.
evidence: This describes the methods used to assess editing outcomes.

claim: Initial electroporation conditions with Cas9 RNPs targeting AAVS1 and TNF showed efficient genome editing, but editing of TLR4 was inefficient.
source: By testing a grid of electroporation conditions, we identified conditions with efficient genome editing of AAVS1 and TNF and limited toxicity, but editing of TLR4 was inefficient (Figure 1b,c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the genotyping data shown in the figures.

claim: The large majority of observed indels were 1 or 2 bp deletions, which are frameshift mutations that eliminate the function of the gene.
source: The large majority of observed indels were 1 or 2 bp deletions (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), which are frameshift mutations that eliminate the function of the gene.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data shown in the figures.

claim: To improve editing efficiency, the authors leveraged sgRNA design tools optimized for RNP activity and targeted each locus with two to three sgRNAs with binding sites tiled across a 200 bp stretch.
source: To improve editing efficiency, we (i) leveraged sgRNA design tools optimized for RNP activity (CRISPR Design Tool, Synthego) and (ii) targeted each locus with two to three sgRNAs with binding sites tiled across a 200 bp stretch to induce simultaneous double-strand breaks
evidence: This describes the strategy used to improve editing efficiency.

claim: The multi-sgRNA design increases the likelihood of achieving functional knockouts by preventing error-free DNA repair and/or removing a stretch of the gene.
source: a design that increases the likelihood of achieving functional knockouts by preventing error-free DNA repair and/or removing a stretch of the gene (Materials and methods) (Riggan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and the rationale for the design.

claim: The authors devised a scheme to correct sequencing counts for length differences to the WT locus to accurately quantify editing efficiency.
source: Because such large deletions generate smaller amplicons in our genotyping approach, which may be overrepresented in sequencing counts due to length biases in PCR amplification and the sequencing reaction itself, we devised a scheme to correct sequencing counts for length differences to the WT locus to accurately quantify editing efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation to address a technical challenge.

claim: Testing the multi-sgRNA approach across three loci revealed a shift in indel profiles toward large deletions and multiple indels with deletions of sequences between sgRNA cut sites as well as a modest increase in editing efficiency.
source: Testing the multi-sgRNA approach across three loci revealed a shift in indel profiles toward large deletions and multiple indels with deletions of sequences between sgRNA cut sites as well as a modest increase in editing efficiency (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This is supported by the genotyping data shown in the figures.

claim: Cas9 RNPs assembled with sgRNAs rather than with crRNA:tracrRNA duplexes mediated higher editing efficiency.
source: Cas9 RNPs assembled with sgRNAs rather than with crRNA:tracrRNA duplexes mediated higher editing efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative genotyping data shown in the figure.

claim: Through an expansive grid search of electroporation conditions, the authors identified a condition (P3, DJ108) with editing efficiencies >90%, high cell recovery, and high specificity in detecting loss of TNF-α secretion upon stimulation with LPS from E. coli O55 after knockout of TNF or TLR4 but not CXCR4.
source: Through an expansive grid search of electroporation conditions, we next identified a condition (P3, DJ108) with editing efficiencies >90%, high cell recovery, and high specificity in detecting loss of TNF-α secretion upon stimulation with LPS from E. coli O55 (E. coli LPS) after knockout of TNF or the LPS receptor TLR4 (Poltorak et al., 1998) but not CXCR4, a chemokine receptor not involved in LPS signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the optimization data shown in the figure.

claim: TLR4 is the LPS receptor.
source: the LPS receptor TLR4 (Poltorak et al., 1998)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CXCR4 is a chemokine receptor not involved in LPS signaling.
source: but not CXCR4, a chemokine receptor not involved in LPS signaling
evidence: This is established knowledge about CXCR4 function.

claim: Benchmarking the procedure for 10 genes in moDCs derived from three independent donors revealed editing efficiencies >80% for all genes and >90% for most genes.
source: Benchmarking the procedure for 10 genes in moDCs derived from three independent donors revealed editing efficiencies >80% for all genes and >90% for most genes (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the genotyping data shown in the figures.

claim: TNF-α is induced by MYD88 and TRIF (TICAM1) downstream of TLR4.
source: (i) TNF-α, which is induced by MYD88 and TRIF (TICAM1) downstream of TLR4
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR4 signaling pathways supported by citations in the text.

claim: CXCL10 (IP-10) is induced by TRIF via activation of IRF3 and production of interferon beta (IFNB1), independently of MYD88.
source: and (ii) CXCL10 (IP-10), which is induced by TRIF via activation of IRF3 and production of interferon beta (IFNB1), independently of MYD88 (Fitzgerald et al., 2003; Fitzgerald and Kagan, 2020; Yamamoto et al., 2003; Yamamoto et al., 2002)
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR4 signaling pathways supported by citations.

claim: TLR4 knockout abolished production of both TNF-α and CXCL10.
source: TLR4 knockout abolished production of both TNF-α and CXCL10
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Knockout of MYD88 or TNF reduced TNF-α production and mildly increased CXCL10 production in at least one donor.
source: knockout of MYD88 or TNF reduced TNF-α production (and mildly increased CXCL10 production in at least one donor)
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: TICAM1 knockout strongly reduced CXCL10 production and moderately reduced TNF-α production.
source: TICAM1 knockout strongly reduced CXCL10 production and moderately reduced TNF-α production
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Knockout of IFNB1 or IRF3 only reduced CXCL10 production.
source: and knockout of IFNB1 or IRF3 only reduced CXCL10 production (Figure 1g, Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in the figures.

claim: The effect of knocking out IRF3 was weak, perhaps due to redundancy with other transcription factors such as IRF7 or due to incomplete protein depletion.
source: The effect of knocking out IRF3 was weak, perhaps due to redundancy with other transcription factors such as IRF7 or due to incomplete protein depletion.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the weak phenotype of IRF3 knockout.

claim: Knockout of TNF or MYD88 reduced the response to both E. coli LPS and Pam3CSK4.
source: knockout of TNF or MYD88 reduced the response to both stimuli
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Knockout of TLR4 or TLR2 only reduced the responses to their cognate ligands.
source: whereas knockout of TLR4 or TLR2 only reduced the responses to their cognate ligands (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data showing ligand-specific effects.

claim: The moDC genome editing strategy enables the detection of functional consequences of knockouts, demonstrating that protein depletion can be effected without perturbing the ability of moDCs to respond to innate immune stimuli.
source: Thus, our moDC genome editing strategy enables the detection of functional consequences of knockouts, demonstrating that we can effect protein depletion without perturbing the ability of moDCs to respond to innate immune stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data showing expected phenotypes for known genes.

claim: Staining patterns for DC markers were qualitatively indistinguishable for moDCs with knockout of B2M or RPE65, moDCs electroporated with a non-targeting control sgRNA, or unedited moDCs that had been cultured alongside the knockout moDCs in 96-well plates.
source: Staining patterns were qualitatively indistinguishable for moDCs with knockout of B2M or RPE65, moDCs electroporated with a non-targeting control sgRNA, or unedited moDCs (no electroporation/no RNP control) that had been cultured alongside the knockout moDCs in 96-well plates (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in the figure.

claim: Both knockout and unedited moDCs from 96-well plates had mildly elevated levels of HLA-DR and B2M compared to unedited moDCs that had been cultured in flasks, indicating that culture conditions can affect DC state independent of editing.
source: Both knockout and unedited moDCs from 96-well plates had mildly elevated levels of HLA-DR and B2M compared to unedited moDCs that had been cultured in flasks, indicating that culture conditions can affect DC state independent of editing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data comparing different culture conditions.

claim: B2M staining was reduced 72% and 65% in B2M knockout moDCs for the two donors, consistent with protein depletion.
source: Although our antibody panel was not designed for precise measurements of B2M levels, B2M staining was reduced 72% and 65% in B2M knockout moDCs for the two donors, consistent with protein depletion.
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data showing reduced B2M staining in B2M knockout cells.

claim: The editing strategy does not perturb DC state.
source: Together, these data provide evidence that our editing strategy does not perturb DC state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry data showing similar marker expression in edited and unedited cells.

claim: Humans are colonized by trillions of Gram-negative microbes that generate milligram to gram quantities of LPS in the intestinal tracts without tonic inflammation.
source: Despite LPS being a classic inflammatory molecule, humans are colonized by trillions of Gram-negative microbes that generate milligram to gram quantities of LPS in the intestinal tracts without tonic inflammation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the human microbiome and LPS.

claim: The lack of tonic inflammation despite high LPS levels has been attributed in part to the different chemical structures and immunomodulatory activities of LPSs from commensal Bacteroidetes compared to the canonical inflammatory LPSs from E. coli and related Proteobacteria.
source: This observation has been attributed in part to the different chemical structures and immunomodulatory activities of LPSs from commensal Bacteroidetes, among the most common Gram-negative phyla in the guts of western individuals (Wexler and Goodman, 2017), compared to the canonical inflammatory LPSs from E. coli and related Proteobacteria (Coats et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2015; Vatanen et al., 2016; d'Hennezel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on LPS structure and activity.

claim: Bacteroidetes are among the most common Gram-negative phyla in the guts of western individuals.
source: among the most common Gram-negative phyla in the guts of western individuals (Wexler and Goodman, 2017)
evidence: This is established knowledge about the human microbiome supported by citation.

claim: The Bacteroidetes-to-Proteobacteria LPS ratio in the gut microbiome has been associated with the incidence of type 1 diabetes.
source: Indeed, the Bacteroidetes-to-Proteobacteria LPS ratio in the gut microbiome has been associated with the incidence of type 1 diabetes (Vatanen et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on microbiome and disease.

claim: LPSs from the human microbiome contribute to shaping immune function.
source: suggesting that LPSs from the human microbiome contribute to shaping immune function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association between LPS ratios and disease.

claim: The biological activities of LPSs from gut Bacteroidetes have remained controversial as they have been reported to be both TLR4 antagonists and agonists.
source: The biological activities of LPSs from gut Bacteroidetes, however, have remained controversial as they have been reported to be both TLR4 antagonists and agonists (d'Hennezel et al., 2017; Steimle et al., 2019; Vatanen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting reports in the literature.

claim: B. theta is an abundant member of the human gut microbiota whose LPS biosynthetic machinery has been characterized.
source: We focused on LPS from B. theta, an abundant member of the human gut microbiota whose LPS biosynthetic machinery has been characterized, allowing us to genetically manipulate its structure (Coats et al., 2011; Cullen et al., 2015; Jacobson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on B. theta.

claim: The characterized LPS biosynthetic machinery of B. theta allows genetic manipulation of its structure.
source: allowing us to genetically manipulate its structure (Coats et al., 2011; Cullen et al., 2015; Jacobson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on B. theta LPS engineering.

claim: Human moDCs stimulated with B. theta LPS secreted moderate levels of TNF-α; this response was weaker than that elicited by E. coli LPS both in magnitude and apparent EC50 but substantially stronger than that elicited by Rhodobacter sphaeroides LPS.
source: Human moDCs stimulated with B. theta LPS secreted moderate levels of TNF-α as quantified by ELISA; this response was weaker than that elicited by E. coli LPS both in magnitude and apparent EC50 but substantially stronger than that elicited by Rhodobacter sphaeroides LPS, a well-characterized TLR4 antagonist (Figure 2a; Golenbock et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Rhodobacter sphaeroides LPS is a well-characterized TLR4 antagonist.
source: Rhodobacter sphaeroides LPS, a well-characterized TLR4 antagonist (Figure 2a; Golenbock et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Although the pattern of response to B. theta LPS was consistent across moDCs from independent donors, response magnitude and EC50 varied by sixfold and >20-fold, respectively.
source: Although the pattern was consistent across moDCs from independent donors, response magnitude and EC50 varied by sixfold and >20-fold, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is supported by the dose-response data across multiple donors.

claim: Donor-specific factors shape immune responses to LPS.
source: even for moDCs processed in parallel, suggesting that donor-specific factors shape immune responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variation in responses across donors.

claim: Analysis of the transcriptional responses of moDCs by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq confirmed that B. theta LPS activated both MYD88 and TRIF signaling more weakly than E. coli LPS, with a more pronounced difference for TRIF signaling.
source: Analysis of the transcriptional responses of moDCs by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq confirmed that B. theta LPS activated both MYD88 and TRIF signaling more weakly than E. coli LPS, with a more pronounced difference for TRIF signaling, again with donor-to-donor variation (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR and RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: There is donor-to-donor variation in transcriptional responses to B. theta LPS.
source: again with donor-to-donor variation (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR and RNA-seq data across multiple donors.

claim: LPSs of Bacteroidetes generally contain pentaacylated, monophosphorylated lipid A as opposed to the hexaacylated, diphosphorylated lipid A of Proteobacteria.
source: LPSs of Bacteroidetes generally contain pentaacylated, monophosphorylated lipid A as opposed to the hexaacylated, diphosphorylated lipid A of Proteobacteria (Coats et al., 2011; Weintraub et al., 1989)
evidence: This is established knowledge about LPS structure supported by citations.

claim: B. theta LPS modified to contain pentaacylated, diphosphorylated lipid A has increased capacity to stimulate TLR4 signaling via the endocytotic pathway.
source: A previous study had established that B. theta LPS modified to contain pentaacylated, diphosphorylated lipid A has increased capacity to stimulate TLR4 signaling via the endocytotic pathway (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: B. theta 4PP LPS elicited substantially lower levels of TNF-α production and smaller transcriptional responses than B. theta WT LPS, with barely detectable responses in some donors.
source: B. theta 4PP LPS elicited substantially lower levels of TNF-α production and smaller transcriptional responses than B. theta WT LPS, with barely detectable responses in some donors (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA and RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: B. theta LPS is a partial TLR4 agonist whose immunostimulatory activity can be tuned by rational engineering.
source: Thus, B. theta LPS is a partial TLR4 agonist whose immunostimulatory activity can be tuned by rational engineering.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing intermediate activity of B. theta WT LPS and reduced activity of B. theta 4PP LPS.

claim: TLR4 knockout moDCs did not secrete detectable amounts of TNF-α in response to E. coli LPS but secreted substantial amounts of TNF-α in response to B. theta LPS, corresponding to 30–50% of the levels secreted by moDCs with knockout of the neutral control gene RPE65.
source: TLR4 knockout moDCs did not secrete detectable amounts of TNF-α in response to E. coli LPS but secreted substantial amounts of TNF-α in response to B. theta LPS, corresponding to 30–50% of the levels secreted by moDCs with knockout of the neutral control gene RPE65 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in the figure.

claim: Receptors other than TLR4 contribute to recognition of B. theta LPS.
source: These results suggest that receptors other than TLR4 contribute to recognition of B. theta LPS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TLR4 knockout cells retain partial response to B. theta LPS.

claim: The genome editing procedure does not perturb DC state, as evidenced by transcriptional profiles of knockout moDCs being similar to unedited moDCs.
source: First, to further assess if our genome editing procedure perturbs DC state, we compared the transcriptional profiles of mock-treated moDCs with knockout of RPE65 from two independent donors from this experiment (donors p and q) to the profiles of unedited moDCs from a previous experiment (donors r and s). Transcriptional profiles segregated primarily by donor, and each of the profiles of knockout moDCs more closely resembled those of unedited moDCs from one donor than the profiles of unedited moDCs from different donors resembled each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing that donor identity is the primary source of variation.

claim: Knockout moDCs had similar expression levels for a panel of DC and myeloid cell markers compared to unedited moDCs.
source: Knockout moDCs also had similar expression levels for a panel of DC and myeloid cell markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claim: TLR4 knockout abolished the response to E. coli O55 LPS.
source: Whereas TLR4 knockout abolished the response to E. coli O55 LPS
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2e.

claim: TLR4 knockout moDCs retained a partial transcriptional response to B. theta WT LPS corresponding to activation of MYD88, but not TRIF.
source: TLR4 knockout moDCs retained a partial transcriptional response to B. theta WT LPS corresponding to activation of MYD88, but not TRIF (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d,e).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claim: The authors designed a focused library targeting ~300 genes including known and predicted pattern recognition receptors and multiple nodes of signaling pathways downstream of each receptor class.
source: To identify additional factors that contribute to recognition of B. theta LPS, we leveraged our moDC editing strategy to conduct an arrayed genetic screen (Figure 3a). We designed a focused library targeting ~300 genes including known and predicted pattern recognition receptors and multiple nodes of signaling pathways downstream of each receptor class (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the design of the genetic screen library.

claim: Editing efficiency was high in both donors in the genetic screen, with median efficiencies of 94.2% and 97.6%.
source: Editing efficiency was high in both donors, with median efficiencies of 94.2% and 97.6% (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by the genotyping data from the screen.

claim: TNF-α secretion was generally unaffected for genes with editing efficiency <75%, suggesting a low false-positive rate.
source: TNF-α secretion was generally unaffected for genes with editing efficiency <75%, suggesting a low false-positive rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b)
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between editing efficiency and phenotype.

claim: The authors identified 37 genes for which knockout altered TNF-α secretion for one donor and 41 genes for the second donor.
source: We identified 37 genes for which knockout altered TNF-α secretion for one donor ('donor h') and 41 genes for the second donor ('donor i'), with altered secretion defined as an absolute log2 fold-change in TNF-α levels ≥2 standard deviations from 0 (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 5a–c, standard deviations calculated based on the log2 fold-changes for all neutral genes, see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in the figures.

claim: For each donor in the screen, altered TNF-α secretion was observed for all four wells targeting the positive control gene TNF and one well targeting a neutral control gene (of 36 such wells).
source: For each donor, we observed altered TNF-α secretion for all four wells targeting the positive control gene TNF and one well targeting a neutral control gene (of 36 such wells).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data and indicates the specificity of the screen.

claim: Knockout of 15 genes (including TNF) impacted TNF-α secretion in response to B. theta WT LPS in both donors.
source: Knockout of 15 genes (including TNF) impacted TNF-α secretion in response to B. theta WT LPS in both donors.
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Knockouts in the TLR4 signaling pathway strongly reduced TNF-α secretion, including TLR4 and its co-receptor MD2 (LY96), CD14, as well as genes involved in MYD88 signaling, the branch of TRIF signaling involved in NF-κB activation, and the NF-κB factor RELA.
source: Knockouts in the TLR4 signaling pathway strongly reduced TNF-α secretion, including TLR4 and its co-receptor MD2 (LY96), CD14 (which delivers LPS to TLR4 and initiates TLR4 endocytosis [Zanoni et al., 2011]), as well as genes involved in MYD88 signaling, the branch of TRIF signaling involved in NF-κB activation, and the NF-κB factor RELA (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in the figure.

claim: CD14 delivers LPS to TLR4 and initiates TLR4 endocytosis.
source: CD14 (which delivers LPS to TLR4 and initiates TLR4 endocytosis [Zanoni et al., 2011])
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: 6 and 7 of the 10 targeted genes in MYD88 signaling reduced TNF-α secretion in the two donors, with knockout of most of the remaining genes causing a less substantial reduction in TNF-α secretion.
source: Indeed, 6 and 7 of the 10 targeted genes in MYD88 signaling reduced TNF-α secretion in the two donors, with knockout of most of the remaining genes causing a less substantial reduction in TNF-α secretion (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in the figure.

claim: moDCs with knockout of A20 (TNFAIP3), which inhibits LPS- and TNF-α-induced NF-κB signaling, secreted more TNF-α.
source: Other knockouts also caused expected phenotypes; for example, moDCs with knockout of A20 (TNFAIP3), which inhibits LPS- and TNF-α-induced NF-κB signaling, secreted more TNF-α (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 5c).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data and is consistent with the known function of A20.

claim: A20 (TNFAIP3) inhibits LPS- and TNF-α-induced NF-κB signaling.
source: A20 (TNFAIP3), which inhibits LPS- and TNF-α-induced NF-κB signaling
evidence: This is established knowledge about A20 function.

claim: Knockouts of PTPN6 (SHP-1) and to a lesser extent IL10 increased TNF-α secretion in response to B. theta WT LPS in one donor but not the other.
source: Most prominently, knockouts of PTPN6 (SHP-1) and to a lesser extent IL10 increased TNF-α secretion in response to B. theta WT LPS in one donor ('donor i') but not the other ('donor h'), suggesting that these factors can suppress TNF-α secretion in response to LPS stimulation in a manner that differs among individuals (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data showing donor-specific effects.

claim: PTPN6 and IL10 can suppress TNF-α secretion in response to LPS stimulation in a manner that differs among individuals.
source: suggesting that these factors can suppress TNF-α secretion in response to LPS stimulation in a manner that differs among individuals (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the donor-specific effects observed in the screen.

claim: Unedited moDCs from donor i secreted less TNF-α in response to both B. theta WT LPS and E. coli LPS than those from donor h.
source: Indeed, unedited moDCs from donor i secreted less TNF-α in response to both B. theta WT LPS and E. coli LPS than those from donor h (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by the dose-response data shown in the figure.

claim: MYD88 signaling contributed particularly strongly to the response to B. theta WT LPS for donor h.
source: Second, MYD88 signaling contributed particularly strongly to the response to B. theta WT LPS for donor h: knockout of TIRAP, the TLR4-proximal adapter for MYD88 signaling (Fitzgerald et al., 2001; Fitzgerald and Kagan, 2020), induced the strongest decrease in TNF-α secretion other than TNF itself.
evidence: This is supported by the screen data showing strong effect of TIRAP knockout in donor h.

claim: TIRAP is the TLR4-proximal adapter for MYD88 signaling.
source: TIRAP, the TLR4-proximal adapter for MYD88 signaling (Fitzgerald et al., 2001; Fitzgerald and Kagan, 2020)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: For donor i, TLR4 and the TRIF pathway contributed more strongly to the response to B. theta LPS, as evidenced by strong decreases in TNF-α secretion upon knockout of TLR4 alone, TRAM (TICAM2), and TRIF (TICAM1).
source: For donor i, TLR4 and the TRIF pathway contributed more strongly to the response, as evidenced by strong decreases in TNF-α secretion upon knockout of TLR4 alone, TRAM (TICAM2), and TRIF (TICAM1) (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data showing strong effects of these knockouts in donor i.

claim: Differences in the relative contributions of MYD88 and TRIF pathways account for many of the donor-specific hits in the screen.
source: These differences account for many of the donor-specific hits (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 5c).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of donor-specific effects in the screen.

claim: A separate 40-gene validation experiment with cells from two additional, independent donors recapitulated the screen results, with results from each of the two validation donors aligning more closely with those from one of the initial donors.
source: A separate 40-gene validation experiment with cells from two additional, independent donors recapitulated these results, with results from each of the two validation donors aligning more closely with those from one of the initial donors (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in the figure.

claim: TLR2 is canonically known as a receptor for lipopeptides and teichoic acids.
source: We focused on TLR2, canonically known as a receptor for lipopeptides and teichoic acids
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR2 function.

claim: TLR2 has been implicated in the response to non-proteobacterial LPSs, although these claims remain controversial.
source: because TLR2 has been implicated in the response to non-proteobacterial LPSs (Di Lorenzo et al., 2020; Werts et al., 2001), although these claims remain controversial.
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature, with acknowledgment of controversy.

claim: moDCs with simultaneous knockout of TLR4 and TLR2 exhibited the strongest decreases in TNF-α secretion among all samples for both donors.
source: Indeed, moDCs with simultaneous knockout of TLR4 and TLR2 exhibited the strongest decreases in TNF-α secretion among all samples for both donors (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in the figures.

claim: Knockout of TLR2 alone reduced the response to B. theta WT LPS but not to E. coli LPS in a donor in the validation experiment.
source: In addition, knockout of TLR2 alone reduced the response to B. theta WT LPS but not to E. coli LPS in a donor in our validation experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 6b).
evidence: This is supported by the validation data shown in the figure.

claim: The results are consistent with the possibility that TLR2 contributes to the response to B. theta LPS, although the presence of contaminating lipopeptides in the LPS preparation cannot be ruled out.
source: These results are consistent with the possibility that TLR2 contributes to the response to B. theta LPS, although we cannot rule out the presence of contaminating lipopeptides in our LPS preparation.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the TLR2 data, acknowledging alternative explanations.

claim: The effects of knockouts on TNF-α and IL-10 secretion were well correlated, suggesting that TLR4 signaling via the TRIF and MYD88 branches accounts for secretion of both TNF-α and IL-10.
source: The effects of knockouts on TNF-α and IL-10 secretion were well correlated, suggesting that TLR4 signaling via the TRIF and MYD88 branches accounts for secretion of both TNF-α and IL-10.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between TNF-α and IL-10 levels across knockouts.

claim: PTPN6 stood out as an exception: whereas PTPN6 knockout strongly increased TNF-α secretion, it moderately decreased IL-10 secretion.
source: PTPN6 stood out as an exception: whereas PTPN6 knockout strongly increased TNF-α secretion, it moderately decreased IL-10 secretion (Figure 3g)
evidence: This is supported by the ELISA data shown in the figure.

claim: IL-10 acts upstream of PTPN6 in suppressing TNF-α secretion or PTPN6 specifically inhibits production of TNF-α and not IL-10.
source: suggesting either that IL-10 acts upstream of PTPN6 in suppressing TNF-α secretion or that PTPN6 specifically inhibits production of TNF-α and not IL-10.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on the differential effects of PTPN6 knockout on TNF-α and IL-10.

claim: Combining the moDC editing strategy with multiple readouts can increase the resolution in evaluating immune response pathways.
source: More broadly, these results demonstrate how combining our moDC editing strategy with multiple readouts can increase the resolution in evaluating immune response pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the insights gained from measuring both TNF-α and IL-10.

claim: The CRISPR strategy is efficient and consistent, with median knockout efficiencies of >94% across >300 genes in two independent donors and comparable efficiencies at smaller scales across >10 further donors.
source: First, our strategy is efficient and consistent, with median knockout efficiencies of >94% across >300 genes in two independent donors and comparable efficiencies at smaller scales across >10 further donors.
evidence: This is supported by the genotyping data from the screen and other experiments.

claim: The knockouts are introduced directly in differentiated DCs, reducing the potential for batch effects that may occur when introducing knockouts in precursor populations prior to differentiation.
source: Second, the knockouts are introduced directly in differentiated DCs, reducing the potential for batch effects that may occur when introducing knockouts in precursor populations prior to differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the approach based on the experimental design.

claim: Any gene is in principle targetable in the strategy, including genes required for DC differentiation.
source: As a corollary, any gene is in principle targetable in our strategy, including for example genes required for DC differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference about the capabilities of the method based on editing in differentiated cells.

claim: The strategy is compatible with a variety of readouts to interrogate the phenotypes of knockout moDCs, including cytokine profiling, RNA-seq, flow cytometry, microscopy, and co-culture assays.
source: Third, our strategy is compatible with a variety of readouts to interrogate the phenotypes of knockout moDCs, including cytokine profiling, RNA-seq, flow cytometry, microscopy, and co-culture assays, enabling dissection of DC biology at high resolution.
evidence: This is supported by the various assays performed in the manuscript.

claim: As a result of the high efficiency and elimination of batch effects, the strategy enables genetic screens at previously intractable scales of hundreds of genes and would readily scale further with access to automation.
source: Fourth, as a result of the high efficiency and elimination of batch effects, our strategy enables genetic screens at previously intractable scales of hundreds of genes and would readily scale further with access to automation.
evidence: This is an inference about the capabilities of the method based on the screen results.

claim: Because human DCs do not divide in culture, the strategy relies on degradation to deplete protein molecules produced before genome editing.
source: First, because human DCs do not divide in culture, our strategy relies on degradation to deplete protein molecules produced before genome editing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC biology and an inference about the mechanism of protein depletion.

claim: Strong phenotypes are observed after targeting immune receptors and few false negatives are observed in the MYD88 pathway in the screen, suggesting that most proteins are depleted during the 5-day period after electroporation.
source: We observe strong phenotypes after targeting immune receptors and few false negatives in the MYD88 pathway in our screen, suggesting that most proteins are depleted during the 5-day period after electroporation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results showing expected phenotypes.

claim: Depleting exceptionally long-lived proteins would require prolonged culture, which may not be experimentally feasible.
source: Nonetheless, depleting exceptionally long-lived proteins would require prolonged culture, which may not be experimentally feasible.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential limitation of the method.

claim: As an RNP-based strategy, the strategy is not readily compatible with pooled screening because no sgRNA barcodes are inserted into the genome.
source: Second, as an RNP-based strategy, our strategy is not readily compatible with pooled screening because no sgRNA barcodes are inserted into the genome.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of the RNP-based approach.

claim: This limitation has been circumvented in T-cells by combining lentiviral sgRNA delivery and Cas9 electroporation.
source: This limitation has been circumvented in T-cells by combining lentiviral sgRNA delivery and Cas9 electroporation (Shifrut et al., 2018; Ting et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in T cells.

claim: Implementation of lentiviral sgRNA delivery combined with Cas9 electroporation in DCs is hampered by the recalcitrance of DCs to lentivirus infection and the tendency of DCs to undergo maturation when infection is forced.
source: Implementation of such a strategy in DCs is hampered by the recalcitrance of DCs to lentivirus infection and the tendency of DCs to undergo maturation when infection is forced, such as by co-transduction of Vpx, but may become feasible with the development of transduction strategies for DCs.
evidence: This is an inference about challenges in adapting the T cell approach to DCs based on known properties of DCs.

claim: It is difficult to knock out highly homologous genes using CRISPR methods because of challenges in designing sgRNAs that are both active and specific.
source: Third, as for any CRISPR method, it is difficult to knock out highly homologous genes, such as some C-type lectin receptors, because of challenges in designing sgRNAs that are both active and specific.
evidence: This is established knowledge about a general limitation of CRISPR methods.

claim: The genetic screen broadly recapitulates known LPS signaling pathways.
source: Indeed, our genetic screen broadly recapitulates known LPS signaling pathways
evidence: This is supported by the screen data showing expected hits in known pathways.

claim: There is a potential contribution of TLR2 to signaling by B. theta LPS.
source: First, we observe a potential contribution of TLR2 to signaling by B. theta LPS, as has also been proposed for B. vulgatus LPS (Di Lorenzo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data and validation experiments, with citation to similar findings for B. vulgatus.

claim: The observation of TLR2 contribution could result from either an intrinsic ability of B. theta LPS to bind both TLR4 and TLR2 or the presence of contaminating TLR2 ligands in the B. theta LPS preparation.
source: This observation could result from either an intrinsic ability of B. theta LPS to bind both TLR4 and TLR2 or the presence of contaminating TLR2 ligands in our B. theta LPS preparation, which we have not ruled out.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations for the TLR2 data.

claim: PTPN6/SHP-1 is identified as a potential contributor to inter-individual variation in the response to LPS.
source: Second, we identify PTPN6/SHP-1 as a potential contributor to inter-individual variation in the response to LPS.
evidence: This is supported by the screen data showing donor-specific effects of PTPN6 knockout.

claim: Activation of PTPN6/SHP-1, in addition to regulating innate immunity, suppresses antigen cross-presentation.
source: Activation of PTPN6/SHP-1, in addition to regulating innate immunity, suppresses antigen cross-presentation (Ding et al., 2016)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Some pathogens exploit PTPN6/SHP-1 to subvert adaptive immunity.
source: which some pathogens exploit to subvert adaptive immunity (Khouili et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Further support for the finding of inter-individual variation in PTPN6/SHP-1 activity would have immediate implications both for understanding variations in pathogen susceptibility and for personalizing DC vaccines aimed at initiating CD8 T-cell responses.
source: Further support for our finding of inter-individual variation in PTPN6/SHP-1 activity thus would have immediate implications both for understanding variations in pathogen susceptibility and for personalizing DC vaccines aimed at initiating CD8 T-cell responses.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential implications of the PTPN6 findings.

claim: Observations of inter-individual variation in immune responses have been reported previously.
source: Our observations of inter-individual variation in immune responses, alongside many previous reports (Brodin and Davis, 2017; Fairfax et al., 2014; Sanz et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on inter-individual variation.

claim: The observations underscore the importance of probing immune responses directly in donor-derived cells.
source: further underscore the importance of probing immune responses directly in donor-derived cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the observed variation.

claim: moDCs from different donors have distinct responses – both in magnitude and apparent affinity – to identical preparations of LPS.
source: For example, moDCs from different donors have distinct responses – both in magnitude and apparent affinity – to identical preparations of LPS.
evidence: This is supported by the dose-response data across multiple donors.

claim: Variation in immune responses likely results from a combination of genetic factors and environmental exposures that together determine immune cell state, with contributions from PTPN6/SHP-1 activity emerging as a hypothesis.
source: Such variation likely results from a combination of genetic factors and environmental exposures that together determine immune cell state, with contributions from PTPN6/SHP-1 activity emerging as a hypothesis from our data.
evidence: This is an inference combining established knowledge with the screen findings.

claim: Longitudinal studies with larger cohorts of donors will be required to dissect the relative contributions of genetic and environmental factors to inter-individual variation and to more clearly define genetic drivers of inter-individual variation.
source: Longitudinal studies with larger cohorts of donors will be required to dissect the relative contributions of these factors and to more clearly define genetic drivers of inter-individual variation
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: The work provides enabling tools for longitudinal studies of inter-individual variation in immunity.
source: and our work now provides enabling tools for such studies.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of the developed method.

claim: Human DCs initiate specific responses to LPS from commensal Bacteroidetes: B. theta LPS induces an inflammatory response that is weaker in both magnitude and apparent EC50 than the response induced by E. coli LPS.
source: Finally, we find that human DCs initiate specific responses to LPS from commensal Bacteroidetes: B. theta LPS induces an inflammatory response that is weaker in both magnitude and apparent EC50 than the response induced by E. coli LPS
evidence: This is supported by the dose-response data comparing B. theta and E. coli LPS.

claim: The inflammatory response to B. theta LPS can be further dampened by rational modifications to the LPS lipid A portion.
source: and can be further dampened by rational modifications to the LPS lipid A portion.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing reduced activity of B. theta 4PP LPS.

claim: Despite donor-to-donor variation in the LPS response, the trends in responses to different LPS types hold across all donors examined.
source: Despite donor-to-donor variation in the LPS response, these trends hold across all donors we examined.
evidence: This is supported by the consistent patterns observed across multiple donors.

claim: The findings challenge the notion that Bacteroides LPSs are innocuous components of the human gut microbiota.
source: Our findings challenge the notion that Bacteroides LPSs are innocuous components of the human gut microbiota
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that B. theta LPS induces inflammatory responses.

claim: Homeostatic, TLR4-dependent induction of IFN-β by B. fragilis LPS contributes to antiviral immunity.
source: as further evidenced by a recent report that homeostatic, TLR4-dependent induction of IFN-β by B. fragilis LPS contributes to antiviral immunity (Stefan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work on B. fragilis LPS.

claim: Variations in LPS structure across gut commensals alter capacity to activate TLR4 and may allow for engagement of new receptors altogether.
source: Variations in LPS structure across gut commensals instead alter capacity to activate TLR4 and may allow for engagement of new receptors altogether
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in responses to different LPS types.

claim: Variations in LPS structure have the potential for neomorphic activities as well as further complexity arising from combinatorial perception.
source: with the potential for neomorphic activities as well as further complexity arising from combinatorial perception (Antebi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms supported by citation.

claim: Commensal LPSs likely contribute to shaping immune responses at the host-microbiome interface.
source: In this fashion, commensal LPSs likely contribute to shaping immune responses at the host-microbiome interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed responses to commensal LPS.

claim: Activation of TLRs by commensal immune ligands including LPS contributes to intestinal homeostasis.
source: Indeed, activation of TLRs by commensal immune ligands including LPS contributes to intestinal homeostasis (Rakoff-Nahoum et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms by which commensal LPS contributes to homeostasis may enable efforts to engineer LPSs with defined immunomodulatory capacities.
source: Understanding the underlying mechanisms, using for example the genetic approaches we describe, may in turn enable efforts to engineer LPSs with defined immunomodulatory capacities, akin to our B. theta 4PP LPS mutant.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The availability of functional genomics tools for human DCs opens the door to systematic functional genomics studies to dissect the roles of DC receptors and signaling pathways in mounting immune responses to commensals, pathogens, or tumor cells.
source: Beyond LPS recognition, the availability of functional genomics tools for human DCs now opens the door to a range of applications including systematic functional genomics studies to dissect the roles of DC receptors and signaling pathways in mounting immune responses to commensals, pathogens, or tumor cells
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the method.

claim: The availability of functional genomics tools for human DCs enables targeted engineering of moDCs for therapeutic interventions such as neoantigen vaccination.
source: and targeted engineering of moDCs for therapeutic interventions such as neoantigen vaccination.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications of the method.
